title: The library of things
instructions: Lee el artículo y elige A, B, C o D. Para responder, atiende a ideas, detalles y actitud del autor.
text:
When my neighbour suggested borrowing a drill instead of buying one, I thought she was making a point about saving money. She was, but she was also introducing me to the neighbourhood's new Library of Things. For a modest fee, members could borrow tools, camping equipment and even a sewing machine. I joined because I needed the drill for a single afternoon.

The project began in a vacant shop. Its founders had expected the usual problems: finding money, organising volunteers and checking that equipment was returned safely. What surprised them was how much time people spent in the shop simply asking one another for advice. A member who had come in for a ladder stayed to show someone else how to repair a bicycle. The founders added a monthly repair evening, though they resisted turning every visit into a formal class. People seemed to value the chance to talk as much as the tools.

Not everything worked immediately. The original booking system listed each item without explaining how large it was or what accessories it needed. Members repeatedly arrived to discover that the object they had reserved would not fit in their cars. After a series of complaints, volunteers photographed the equipment and added practical notes to each listing. They also introduced a short safety demonstration for unfamiliar tools. These changes cost little, but they made borrowing far less stressful.

The council later offered the project a larger building. Several members welcomed the extra space; others feared that a move away from the main street would make casual visits less likely. The founders accepted the offer only after the council agreed to fund clear signs and a collection point in the old neighbourhood. Whether that compromise will work remains to be seen. Membership has grown since the move, although it is too early to say whether occasional visitors still feel the same sense of belonging.

I still borrow equipment, but I no longer think of the library simply as a way to avoid buying it. Its most useful lesson may be that sharing requires a little organisation and a willingness to help. That is harder to measure than the number of drills borrowed, and perhaps more valuable.

title: The limits of a city’s green promise
instructions: Lee el artículo y elige A, B, C o D. Las preguntas incluyen inferencia, tono y propósito.
text:
For years, the city measured the success of its tree-planting campaign by the number of saplings put into the ground. The figure was easy to announce and easy to celebrate. Unfortunately, it told residents little about whether the trees would still be alive a decade later. When an independent survey found that many plantings had failed, the council initially blamed unusually dry summers. Weather had played a part, but the survey also identified poor soil, inadequate space for roots and a lack of clear responsibility for watering.

The criticism prompted a change in direction. Instead of announcing another ambitious planting target, the council began mapping where trees could realistically thrive. It also surveyed residents about shade, access and maintenance. Some neighbourhoods wanted new trees immediately; others asked why existing trees had been allowed to deteriorate. This was a fair challenge. Planting is visible, whereas caring for an established tree rarely makes a compelling photograph.

The revised plan gives maintenance a larger share of the budget and sets survival rates as a measure of success. That is an improvement, but it creates a political difficulty. A programme focused on survival may report fewer new trees in its first years, even if it produces a healthier canopy in the long run. Officials will need to explain why a smaller annual planting figure does not necessarily mean reduced ambition. They will also have to publish failures, not just successes, if the new measure is to be trusted.

There is another complication. Trees provide shade and absorb some pollution, but they cannot compensate for every other weakness in urban planning. A narrow street with heavy traffic may require changes to transport as well as greenery. Nor is every empty space suitable for a large tree. The council's own map shows that planting opportunities are unevenly distributed, reflecting decades of unequal investment. The plan acknowledges this, though it has yet to set out how the imbalance will be addressed.

The strongest part of the new approach is its willingness to replace a simple number with a more demanding question: are residents actually gaining healthier, cooler streets? Whether the council can maintain that focus when the next easy headline appears is still uncertain.

title: Four views on a public data portal
instructions: Lee las cuatro opiniones y responde con A–D. Se comparan posturas entre autores.
text:
A — Noor Patel, local journalist: Making council data public is welcome, but a spreadsheet without context can mislead. The portal should explain how figures were collected and what they leave out. Journalists can help interpret the data, provided they resist treating every fluctuation as a scandal.

B — Elena Morris, software developer: The portal’s greatest value lies in allowing citizens to ask questions that officials did not anticipate. Standard descriptions are useful, but the council should not delay publication until every dataset is perfect. Publishing early and correcting openly is preferable to keeping information hidden.

C — Daniel Rowe, community organiser: Residents with limited digital access will not benefit simply because a website exists. The council should use local meetings and printed summaries as well. Like Noor, I worry that figures without explanation may be misunderstood, especially when neighbourhoods are compared.

D — Priya Singh, council analyst: We should publish more, but accuracy matters. A poorly checked dataset can damage trust and is difficult to correct once copied elsewhere. I disagree with Elena’s argument for early release: some internal validation must come first. However, that process should be documented so it does not become an excuse for endless delay.

title: Changing careers: four accounts
instructions: Relaciona cada afirmación con A–D. Las respuestas exigen distinguir motivos y actitudes.
text:
A — Isabelle: I left a secure office role to train as an electrician. Friends assumed I wanted a dramatic break, but I had been volunteering on home repairs for years. The training was demanding, particularly the maths, yet I valued the clear link between a problem and a practical solution. I miss the predictable salary more than the work itself.

B — Tomas: When my company closed, I began teaching adults to use digital services. At first I treated the change as temporary. Then a learner told me she could book her own medical appointments for the first time. That moment made the work feel significant. I still use many skills from my previous job, especially explaining unfamiliar processes clearly.

C — Leila: I moved from restaurant management into environmental research. The subject had long interested me, but I underestimated how long it would take to qualify. I do not regret the decision, although I would advise others to speak to people already working in the field before enrolling. Their everyday experience is more revealing than course advertising.

D — Ben: I had hoped a career change would solve my frustration at work. I trained in graphic design and enjoyed the course, but freelance life brought a different kind of pressure. I have since returned to an employed role that combines design with customer support. The experience taught me to identify what I disliked about a job before assuming the profession itself was wrong.

title: Designing a public archive
instructions: Escucha la charla y completa las frases con la información que falta.
segments: When our team began designing the public archive, we assumed that the main challenge would be digitising old photographs. In fact, identifying the people and places shown in them proved more difficult. We invited former residents to attend weekly identification sessions. Their memories added detail that written records lacked, although we checked each claim against other evidence where possible. The first collection we published focused on the harbour, because it had changed rapidly over the previous fifty years. We then added recorded interviews, but only after obtaining clear consent from speakers. A few participants wanted their names removed from the public version, and we respected that choice. The archive is free to search, while high-resolution image downloads require a modest fee to cover storage costs. Our next task is to improve accessibility for visitors using screen readers. We also plan to publish a guide explaining uncertainty: some photographs can be dated only approximately. What matters is that users understand the difference between a confirmed fact and a reasonable suggestion.

title: Interview with a project evaluator
instructions: Escucha una entrevista y elige A, B, C o D. Presta atención a la actitud y los matices.
segments: Interviewer: You evaluated a scheme that gives young adults access to shared workspaces. Did it succeed? Evaluator: That depends on what we mean by success. Membership grew, and many users valued the quiet space. But the original aim was to help people develop sustainable businesses, and we have limited evidence on that longer-term outcome. Interviewer: Some reports called it a failure. Evaluator: I would not go that far. A shared office cannot by itself solve problems such as lack of finance or childcare. The scheme may be useful, but it needs to be understood as one part of a wider system. Interviewer: What did users tell you? Evaluator: Most praised the facilities, although several said that informal advice from other members mattered even more. That was not something the scheme had planned to provide. Interviewer: Did the organisers respond to your findings? Evaluator: They were initially disappointed by the cautious conclusions. To their credit, they then agreed to track former members and to introduce structured mentoring. Interviewer: Is it difficult to remain independent when people have invested so much in a project? Evaluator: It can be. My responsibility is to explain both benefits and limitations clearly. A flattering report might be easier to write, but it would not help the organisers make better decisions. Interviewer: What would you recommend to a town considering a similar scheme? Evaluator: Set realistic aims, collect evidence from the beginning, and speak to people who could not use the service as well as those who did. Otherwise, a busy building may create an impression of success that hides unmet needs.

title: Five views on change
instructions: Escucha a cinco personas y realiza dos tareas de emparejamiento: motivo principal y actitud final. Sobran opciones.
segments: Speaker 1: Our library replaced a silent reading room with shared tables. I objected because I thought concentration would be impossible. After visiting, I found that a separate quiet area had been preserved. I still prefer the old layout, but my main concern was addressed.

Speaker 2: I supported the new bus route from the start because it links my neighbourhood with the hospital. The first timetable was unreliable, yet the operator listened to complaints and adjusted it. I am pleased they were willing to change rather than defend a weak plan.

Speaker 3: My workplace introduced a digital booking system. I expected it to save time, but many clients struggle with it and staff now spend longer helping them. The company promises training; until I see results, I remain unconvinced.

Speaker 4: The council proposed turning an empty lot into a garden. I volunteered because my children had nowhere nearby to play. The garden is smaller than I imagined, but it has brought neighbours together, which I had not anticipated.

Speaker 5: I joined the museum’s advisory panel because its displays ignored part of our town’s history. The curators took criticism seriously and changed the exhibition. I am proud of the result, although I know the process needs to continue.

instructions: Lee el artículo y elige la mejor respuesta a cada pregunta.
text:
Last year, Mei wanted a hobby she could do after work. She first tried an online painting course, but she found it difficult to keep going alone. Then a friend invited her to a local photography group. Mei was nervous because she had only used her phone camera. The group leader said that was enough for beginners.

At the first meeting, members walked through a park and took pictures of ordinary objects. They showed their photos to one another afterwards. Mei discovered that the same tree looked very different in each person’s picture. She began to notice light and colour more carefully.

The group meets twice a month. Mei now takes photos on her way to work and chooses one to discuss at each meeting. She has bought a simple camera, but she says the most important change was learning to look closely. Next month, she will help organise a small exhibition at the library.

title: The town bicycle project
instructions: Lee el artículo y responde a cinco preguntas.
text:
When the town introduced a shared bicycle scheme, organisers expected most users to be tourists. The first month proved them wrong: local residents made nearly three quarters of all journeys. Many used the bikes for short trips between home, the station and shops.

The scheme was popular, but it faced problems. Some docking stations were full in the morning and empty by the evening. Staff began moving bicycles between stations at busy times. They also added an app showing where bikes were available. This helped users, although people without smartphones still preferred the information boards at each station.

Six months later, a survey found that most members were satisfied. However, several residents said they would use the bikes more if there were safer cycle lanes. The council therefore decided to improve two routes before buying more bicycles. Organiser Grace Lee believes this is the right order: “A good bike is not enough if people do not feel comfortable on the road.”

The project has not reduced car traffic as much as some officials hoped. Nevertheless, it has made short journeys easier for many people. The council will review the scheme again next year, after the new cycle lanes open.
